newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs call for stricter beach monitoring.
newsitem.headline: MEPs call for stricter beach monitoring.

text.p: The European Parliament's environment committee called on Thursday for stricter national controls on the quality of bathing water.

The committee welcomed European Commission plans to update a 21-year-old EU law on bathing water -- COM(94)36 -- but called for further reductions in the maximum permitted levels of sewage, enteroviruses and rubbish.
The committee said the limits should not just apply to water used for swimming but should cover areas used for sailing, surfing and other water sports.
Rapporteur Doeke Eisma tolds Reuters he expected the Council of Ministers to reject this demand but it might eventually force the Commission to propose separate legislation on water sports.
Eisma said the stricter pollution limits which the committee was proposing would make it more expensive for the member states to comply with the revised directive on bathing water quality.

Their record of compliance with existing rules is hardly praiseworthy. Of the 18,000 beaches in the EU covered by the Commission's 1995 bathing water report, more than 3,000 either failed to meet EU minimum requirements on clean water or were not monitored closely enough to determine whether they complied.
Part of the problem was that the list of pollutants the member states were expected to monitor was so long that in some cases they simply did not bother, Eisma, a Dutch Christian Democrat explained.
The Commission is proposing to make their lives easier by dropping from the list a series of substances which it deems do not affect bathers' health directly although they do damage the environment.
These include heavy metals, cyanide, pesticides, ammonia, nitrates and phosphates.
Eisma said he agreed with the Commission's approach.
Other members of the environment committee were less convinced and succeeded in pushing through amendments obliging the member states to monitor nitrate, phosphate and pesticide levels.

In view of the member states' parlous record of compliance with the 1975 directive, the Euro-MPs said there should be more bad publicity to persuade them to monitor and clean up their bathing waters properly.

An accusing finger would be pointed at governments which failed to supply the Commission with a full report every year and polluted areas would not be awarded the EU's blue flag for good quality bathing water, Eisma said.

The environment committee said it also wanted notices posted in all such areas to warn people about pollution and demanded the deletion of a clause which allows the member states to exclude short-lived peaks of pollution from their annual water quality analyses if the pollution subsides within two days and if they inform Brussels.

One of the problems with getting the member states to respect the existing directive is that it gives them too much leeway for deciding which areas they have to monitor and clean up, according to Eisma's report.
The directive's definition of the bathing season is vague and it describes a bathing area as one where there are "a considerable number of bathers".
Eisma's report suggests the directive should cover all areas "where bathing is not prohibited".
The report also recommends introducing harmonised methods for testing water quality, in the form of a code of conduct.
Parliament is expected to approve the environment committee's report at the December 9-11 plenary session under the cooperation procedure.
